Parthenogenesis (/ˌpɑːrθɪnoʊˈdʒɛnɪsɪs, -θɪnə-/; from the Greek παρθένος, parthenos, 'virgin' + γένεσις, genesis, 'creation) is a natural form of asexual reproduction in which growth and development of embryos occur without fertilization by sperm. In animals, parthenogenesis means development of an embryo from an unfertilized egg cell. In plants parthenogenesis is a component process of apomixis.

Parthenogenesis occurs naturally in some plants, some invertebrate animal species (including nematodes, water fleas, some scorpions, aphids, some mites, some bees, some Phasmida and parasitic wasps) and a few vertebrates (such as some fish, amphibians, reptiles and very rarely birds). This type of reproduction has been induced artificially in a few species including fish and amphibians.

Normal egg cells form after meiosis and are haploid, with half as many chromosomes as their mother's body cells. Haploid individuals, however, are usually non-viable, and parthenogenetic offspring usually have the diploid chromosome number. Depending on the mechanism involved in restoring the diploid number of chromosomes, parthenogenetic offspring may have anywhere between all and half of the mother's alleles. The offspring having all of the mother's genetic material are called full clones and those having only half are called half clones. Full clones are usually formed without meiosis. If meiosis occurs, the offspring will get only a fraction of the mother's alleles since crossing over of DNA takes place during meiosis, creating variation.

Parthenogenetic offspring in species that use either the XY or the X0 sex-determination system have two X chromosomes and are female. In species that use the ZW sex-determination system, they have either two Z chromosomes (male) or two W chromosomes (mostly non-viable but rarely a female), or they could have one Z and one W chromosome (female).

We've seen this happen in a number of other species, including a few other vertebrates such as fish, sharks, lizards, and even birds.

The mother determines the sex of the baby because her eggs are all that are available to create the baby.

So in creatures with the XY sex chromosomes, the baby will always be a female because the mother only has Xs to contribute, so the baby is always XX. Female. She has no Y available to make it a male. (The female always contributes X to the baby, and the father contributes either X or Y, and this determines sex in the XY system.)

Each cell in an XY animal has two copies of each chromosome... 1 through 22 and then either an X and X in females, and an X and a Y in males. When sperm and eggs are created in our bodies, they're made by shuffling the DNA between the two copies of each chromosome for the first 22 and then splitting them in half, each half going in a cell with half the DNA, and one of the two sex determining chromosomes. So because all female cells have two Xs, the egg cells always get an X no matter what. So they always contribute an X to the baby. But the father's cells all have X and Y. So he makes half the sperm cells with Xs and half with Ys... because each cell has an X and a Y in it that split into two sperms, each with one of those.

The presence of the Y is what will make a baby a boy. If the baby gets an X from the father, which matches up with the X from the mother, that will make a girl. If the sperm that wins the swimming match has a Y instead, then you get a baby boy.

In those with ZW, it can be male or female because in ZW creatures the females are ZW and males are ZZ, so the females can make ZZ WW and ZW babies depending on which eggs combine.

In the case of ZW creatures, like Komodo dragons, the males are more like the females genetically... they have two copies of the larger Z chromosome (like the X in females in the XY system.) Females in the ZW system are more like males in the XY system. They have one copy of each, and the W is the one that determines the sex. So basically the male sperm always contribute a Z, and it's the egg with either a Z or a W that will determine whether you get a baby boy (ZZ) or girl (ZW.)
